whyThisMatters: If you can name the trick out loud together, you will spot it faster on your own — whether it shows up in a ticket, a vendor call, a system alert, a dependency, a PR comment, or a CI notification. Today's riddles cover the full range of patterns aimed at Technology Team.
rememberThis: This month gave these tricks a name — keep using them. STOP before you install, grant access, reset, merge, or run anything, VERIFY through a channel you already trust, then REPORT.

discussionPrompts: Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up across the combined set now — a fake escalation ticket and PR-comment phishing both hide inside a routine-looking notification, but the goal is different.
Ask for a real example of a ticket, alert, or notification that matches one of these terms.
Ask someone to explain OTP RELAY ATTACK or BROKEN ACCESS CONTROL in their own words, without using the term itself.

Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up now — CONFIDENTIALITY and DATA CLASSIFICATION are related but different: one is the property being protected, the other is the system for deciding how much protection something needs.

Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up now — SECRETS ARCHITECTURE and GIT LIFECYCLE DEFENSE are related but different: one is about where a credential lives, the other is about the process that catches one that leaked anyway.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often mix up categories that share a delivery channel — a fake escalation ticket and PR-comment phishing both arrive as a routine-looking notification; a fake tool alert and a fake vulnerability alert both copy an internal system's exact style. The difference is always in the specific ask: install something, skip a check, merge something, or hand over a credential.

riddles.riddle: I am the three-step habit: 1. STOP before you act, 2. VERIFY using a number or portal you already trust, 3. REPORT to the IT Service Desk. What is this rule called?
I look like a real support ticket, but my sender domain has an extra word, and I ask you to skip change-approval to fix me fast. What trick am I?
I text you right after you process a reset, asking you to read back the one-time code you just received to "verify the action". What trick am I?
I am an unsolicited message inviting you to a coding challenge, and I ask you to run my setup script right away to get started. What trick am I?
I claim your build failed and your deploy credentials expired, and I want you to retype your Git token through my link within 10 minutes. What trick am I?
I say no device or network segment is trusted by default, even inside the perimeter — every request gets verified regardless of where it comes from. What am I?
I'm the four-tier system that decides whether something stays Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted — and how it has to be handled at each level. What am I?
I say a credential belongs in a vault, short-lived and scoped — never hardcoded in source, a frontend bundle, or an unencrypted .env file. What standard am I?
I'm a three-stage defense: a local hook scan before commit, peer review and a signed commit at the pull request, and instant revocation the moment a leak reaches main. What am I?
I'm the discipline that stops a single AI feature from becoming a billing incident — a hard context cap, a per-user rate quota, and a circuit breaker, together. What am I?
